findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the authoritative time source for 'reachable on remote ≥ N days' (e.g. a remote-side receive timestamp or reflog, the S3 bundle object LastModified, or a monotone ancestry anchor) for each backend, and state that commit timestamps alone are not trusted.
evidence: '(C2) that fold reachable on the sync remote's `tickets` ref ≥ N days'
'S1 remote-anchored eligibility — pure git reachability + timestamps.'
findings.finding: The eligibility clock for S1/C2 is unspecified. 'Reachable on the sync remote's tickets ref ≥ N days' requires knowing when a commit became reachable on the remote. Git records only author/committer timestamps, which a drifted clone can push late with old timestamps. The plan says only 'pure git reachability + timestamps' and does not say which timestamp, or how remote-arrival time is established on git remotes versus S3 bundles.
scenarios: A clone offline for 25 days pushes a SNAPSHOT whose committer date is 26 days old. Committer-date eligibility treats it as ≥N on the remote and reclaims inside the real horizon, breaking the <N-day safety argument.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the per-step failure disposition for the S3 replacement (backup failure → abort/retryable with nothing changed; post-write/partial-delete failure → fatal NEEDS_INVESTIGATION + automatic restore from rollback prefix, remote locked).
evidence: "back up the bundle set to a rollback prefix, write ONE rewritten bundle and delete the originals"
No partial-failure disposition is stated
findings.finding: The S3 exclusive replacement is a multi-step, non-atomic sequence: lock, enumerate, back up, write the new bundle, delete the originals. The plan gives no disposition for failure partway through, such as the lock lost or expired, the write succeeding but deletes partially failing, or the backup copy failing. It does not say whether the job rolls forward, restores from the rollback prefix, or halts with a fatal NEEDS_INVESTIGATION state.
findings.location: Feasibility — adapter (b) S3 exclusive bundle-set replacement
scenarios: The new bundle is written but only half the originals are deleted. Clients then see both old and new heads, and the auto-doctor merges them, resurrecting reclaimed history.
The lock expires mid-delete, a client pushes, and its bundle is deleted along with the originals.
findings.suggested_fix: Order the steps as backup (verified), then write new, then delete old. Any failure before the delete aborts as retryable with no change. A failure during the delete restores from the rollback prefix, holds the lock or fences the ref, and surfaces a fatal NEEDS_INVESTIGATION disposition.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the remote-anchored time source for C2 on each backend (not commit timestamps). Examples: the first sync-remote-observed time, recorded on the remote by the receiving side, or S3 bundle LastModified. Prove that eligibility cannot be satisfied by a backdated or offline-authored commit.
evidence: "(C2) that fold reachable on the sync remote's `tickets` ref ≥ N days"
"S1 remote-anchored eligibility — pure git reachability + timestamps."
findings.finding: C2 requires the fold to be 'reachable on the sync remote's `tickets` ref ≥ N days'. S1 computes this from 'pure git reachability + timestamps', but git records no remote-arrival time. Commit and committer timestamps come from the authoring clone's clock and its offline period. A SNAPSHOT folded on a long-offline clone and pushed today carries an old timestamp. It would be judged eligible immediately, although no other clone has had N days to observe it. That violates the remote-anchoring the title and C2 promise.
findings.location: Design + proof C2; Mechanism S1 'remote-anchored eligibility — pure git reachability + timestamps'
scenarios: A clone offline for 35 days compacts locally and then pushes. Its SNAPSHOT committer-date is 35 days old, so S1 marks those events reclaimable at once. A third clone that last synced 10 days ago has unpushed events depending on pre-fold state, and that state is reclaimed under it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Anchor C2 to an arrival time the reclaim tool observes itself, not to committer dates. For example, publish a candidate-boundary/epoch marker onto the remote in one run, and collapse only up to a marker the tool observed on the remote ≥ N days earlier.
evidence: "(C2) that fold reachable on the sync remote's `tickets` ref ≥ N days"
"S1 remote-anchored eligibility — pure git reachability + timestamps"
findings.finding: Eligibility is defined as the fold having been 'reachable on the sync remote's tickets ref ≥ N days', computed by 'pure git reachability + timestamps'. Git records no time at which a commit became reachable on a remote; GitHub, Gerrit and S3 expose no server reflog. The only timestamps available are client-set committer/author dates, which record when the commit was created, not when it reached the remote, and which are subject to clock skew (I8). A clone that commits offline on day 0 and pushes on day 29 produces commits that look 29 days remote-reachable after one day. A clone whose clock runs slow produces commits that are below the horizon the moment they are pushed. C2/C3's convergence guarantee then rests on this proxy.
scenarios: A late push of old-dated commits is collapsed before other clones have fetched it once.
Clock skew makes fresh events look stale, and their clone's unpushed work is classed as accepted loss.
findings.suggested_fix: Make S1 two-phase. Phase A, run periodically, records the remote tip it observed, with the tool's own observation time, as a candidate boundary (a marker on the remote or in the reclaim log). Phase B collapses only up to a candidate boundary whose recorded observation time is ≥ N days old. Committer dates are never the eligibility clock.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the S3 swap's crash semantics. Write a swap journal or marker before mutating anything. Make a re-run detect the {new tip ∪ subset of T0 heads} state and finish the deletions idempotently, or restore from the rollback prefix. Make the auto-doctor skip refs that have an in-progress swap marker. Confirm whether the push lock has a TTL and how it is held across a long upload.
evidence: 'back up the bundle set to a rollback prefix, write ONE rewritten bundle and delete the originals — deliberately BYPASSING the auto-doctor'
'its non-interactive auto-doctor (s3_doctor.py) folds divergent heads by lossless merge and NEVER discards a head, so a normally-pushed rewrite would be MERGED BACK'
'a changed head set aborts+retries' (a re-run after a partial swap would abort, not resume)
findings.finding: The S3 exclusive bundle-set replacement has no partial-failure, resume, or idempotency rules. The plan's order is: back up, write ONE rewritten bundle, delete the originals. If the process crashes or the lock is lost after the new bundle is written but before every original is deleted, the ref holds a mixed head set: the rewritten tip plus some old heads. The non-interactive auto-doctor would then fold those back together by a lossless merge, which is exactly the resurrection the plan is trying to avoid. A plain re-run would also abort, because the head set is no longer T0. The plan does not say whether the per-ref push lock can expire during a long upload, or how a stuck half-finished swap is detected and either completed forward or reverted from the rollback prefix.
findings.location: Feasibility — Publish-swap adapter (b) S3 git-remote-s3 backend
scenarios: The process is killed after uploading the new bundle and deleting 2 of 5 originals. The next client fetch triggers the auto-doctor, which merges the rewritten tip with the 3 surviving old heads, so the old history comes back.
Uploading a multi-hundred-MiB bundle outlasts the push-lock lifetime, and a client push lands while the swap is in progress.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the publish step incremental: when the lease or head-set check fails, fetch T1, replay only T0..T1 onto the already-rewritten tip, and retry against T1 with a bounded loop, holding the S3 lock only for the final short catch-up and swap.
evidence: "replace published history iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry"; "no clone registry, no hold-open window"
"~14K commits/day" (Measured)
S3: "under git-remote-s3's per-ref push-lock, enumerate bundles ... assert the head set == T0"
findings.finding: The publish CAS ('replace published history iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry') will almost never succeed. The tickets branch gets about 14K commits/day, roughly one every 6 seconds, while an offline rewrite of 235K commits/408K trees takes minutes to hours. The --force-with-lease against T0, or the S3 'head set == T0' check, will fail on essentially every attempt. Retrying from scratch just restarts the same race. The only way to make it pass is to hold the S3 push-lock for the whole rewrite, and that is the 'hold-open window' the plan says it avoids.
scenarios: Rewrite built from T0 takes 20 minutes. About 200 commits land in that time, the lease fails, and the retry rebuilds and fails again.
S3: the push-lock is taken only for the swap, the head set has changed, so it aborts. If the lock is held for the whole rebuild, every client's auto-push stalls for that long.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the retry from rebuild-from-scratch to catch-up. Keep the rewritten tip for T0. On CAS failure, fetch the new remote tip T1, replay T0..T1 with commit-tree onto the rewritten tip (cheap, since above-horizon commits are re-parented and otherwise unchanged), and retry with --force-with-lease=refs/heads/tickets:T1. On S3, take the per-ref lock only for the last catch-up, the head-set check, and the bundle replacement, with a bounded attempt count that then backs off.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify an incremental catch-up loop for the publish swap: re-fetch the remote, replay the event files committed since T0 onto the rewritten tip, then retry the CAS against the new T0. Add a bounded retry count and an optional short write-quiesce fallback, so the swap can converge at about 14K commits/day.
evidence: 'replace published history iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry'
'~14K commits/day'
'235,482 commits'
'A rewrite changes every commit SHA'
findings.finding: At the measured write rate, the 'abort+retry' CAS precondition is very likely to fail every time, and the plan has no catch-up step or brief write-freeze. The rewrite re-parents every commit (all 235K, including those inside the horizon) offline, while the remote gains about 14K commits/day (roughly 10/min). By the time the rewritten history is ready, T0 has almost certainly moved, so retrying the whole rewrite livelocks. The plan does not say how commits landing after T0 get carried over (for example, replaying the T0..current delta onto the rewritten tip and re-running the CAS), and it does not bound how long the window is.
findings.location: Feasibility — Publish-swap precondition ('replace published history iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry')
scenarios: The offline fast-import of 235K commits takes minutes to hours. Auto-pushing clones move `tickets` meanwhile, the lease fails, and each retry starts over and fails again.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the rewrite two-phase. Phase 1 collapses the history below the horizon once (slow, offline). Phase 2 is a fast loop: fetch the remote tip T1, replay the event files committed in T0..T1 as new commits on the rewritten tip, then push with --force-with-lease=tickets:T1. Repeat until the push succeeds or K attempts are used up, then escalate to a short quiesce window.

findings.finding: The plan calls the rollback backup 'immutable', but declares no access posture to make it so. It is stored on the shared sync remote, where every authenticated writer clone already has the right to delete it. On S3, the documented writer IAM policy grants s3:DeleteObject on the whole bucket (`arn:aws:s3:::my-org-rebar-tickets/*`), which covers the rollback prefix. On git remotes, any clone with push rights can delete or force-update `refs/tickets-backup/*` unless the server protects that namespace. The one artifact the rollback depends on can therefore be removed by any writer, by mistake or on purpose, during the window before a green Verify Authorship Identity run and full reconcile.

The next doctor run on any client would then merge the whole pre-image history back into the published ref. That undoes the reclaim, brings the pack back to full size, and resurrects old history. git-remote-s3 has no ref CAS to reject such a push.

findings.suggested_fix: Before s3_doctor folds a head, compare its store epoch with the published ref's epoch. If the head is from a superseded epoch, do not merge it. The plan does not cover lock renewal or a TTL override. Separately, its premise that S3 has 'NO ref CAS' is unpinned: upstream now validates remote state under the lock and rejects stale pushes.
scenarios: Uploading a multi-hundred-MiB rewritten bundle takes longer than 60 s. A live clone's auto-push treats the reclaim lock as stale, deletes it, and pushes. The reclaim then deletes the 'original' bundles, including the newly acknowledged one, or leaves multiple bundles that the auto-doctor merges back.
findings.suggested_fix: Before deleting the originals, re-run `get_bundles_for_ref` and abort+rollback if anything other than T0 plus the rewritten bundle exists. Evidence class: Partially-verified. The lock exists, but its exclusivity over a long swap is contradicted by the TTL documented in ADR 0093.
findings.finding: The S3 publish-swap is called 'EXCLUSIVE ... under git-remote-s3's per-ref push-lock', and T0 is checked once at the start. But per ADR 0093, any other client's next push clears that lock as stale after DEFAULT_LOCK_TTL_SECONDS = 60, and the TTL is decided client-side. The swap backs up every original bundle, writes one rewritten bundle for a store of roughly 200–480 MiB, then deletes the originals, which can easily run longer than 60s. If a concurrent auto-push clears the lock mid-swap, its new bundle is not in the enumerated delete set. It survives next to the rewritten bundle, the multi-bundle state triggers the auto-doctor, and the doctor merges the old history back (resurrection). So the claim 'No acknowledged write is lost (a changed head set aborts+retries)' is not guaranteed by the helper.
scenarios: An agent clone auto-pushes 70s into a large S3 swap: it clears the 'stale' lock, uploads `<newsha>.bundle` on top of the old history, the swap deletes only the T0 keys, the doctor later folds both heads, and the pre-rewrite history comes back.
findings.suggested_fix: Do the slow work before locking: copy the T0 bundles to the PROTECTED# rollback prefix and upload the rewritten bundle to a PROTECTED# staging key. Under the lock: enumerate, assert heads == T0, use a server-side S3 CopyObject to move the staged bundle to `<prefix>/<ref>/<new_tip>.bundle`, delete the T0 keys, then re-enumerate and assert the set is exactly {new_key}. Measure elapsed time against the TTL minus a safety margin and abort or roll back if it is exceeded.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make e32d's C2 measure how long the commit has been remotely reachable (for example, the time it first appeared on the remote ref, from a recorded observation), or state in ADR 0106 that committer date is an accepted proxy and record the residual risk.
evidence: Parent C2: 'that fold reachable on the sync remote's `tickets` ref ≥ N days'
e32d plan: 'returns true only when the checkpoint commit is an ancestor of that ref and the checkpoint commit's committer timestamp is at least `[reclaim].horizon_days` old'
e32d: 'evaluates ADR 0106 C3 horizon eligibility'; 'against the current local view of the configured sync remote's tickets ref'
8dc4 boundary: 'git rev-list -1 --first-parent --before=<cutoff> T0' (also based on commit date)
findings.finding: e32d narrows parent C2 ('fold reachable on the sync remote's tickets ref ≥ N days') to 'the checkpoint commit is an ancestor of the local remote-tracking ref AND its committer timestamp is ≥ N days old'. A commit's age does not show how long it has been reachable on the remote. A clone that was offline and pushes late (or merges so that its own old commits land on first-parent) publishes old-dated commits that pass the predicate the moment they arrive. The predicate also reads the local remote-tracking ref without fetching, and it labels itself 'C3' eligibility.
scenarios: A clone drifts 40 days, then merges and pushes. Its 40-day-old commits become reachable on the remote today, are immediately below the horizon, and get collapsed while another clone may still be mid-reconvergence against them.
findings.suggested_fix: Have the eligibility predicate require that the checkpoint was already an ancestor of a remote-ref observation recorded ≥ N days ago (for example, periodically recorded remote-tip snapshots). Otherwise, amend ADR 0106 to accept the committer-date proxy and list late pushes as an accepted residual.

The HARD STOP says none of them is done in this slice. The plan therefore records its empirical validation as complete when it has not been run.
findings.location: Deferred child-slice work (S0–S3) checklist vs HARD STOP
scenarios: An approver or orchestrator reads the checked items as evidence that the resurrection/authorship proofs were empirically validated, and approves the destructive rollout on that basis.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the deferred S0–S3 lines to `- [ ]` (or replace them with links to the child slices) so their completion is tracked where the work happens.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify N as a single configurable setting (e.g. a rebar.toml key) read by both S1 eligibility and S3 stale-clone detection, with S3's threshold never shorter than S1's.
evidence: "Max safe win N=30d ≈ 365–380 MiB; N=7d ≈ 200–215 MiB"
No config key for N is named
findings.finding: The reclamation horizon N=30d is presented as a fixed value, although the plan itself weighs alternatives (N=7d, <4-day). The plan does not say that N is a configurable setting read consistently by S1 eligibility and S3 stale-clone detection.
scenarios: The operator later tightens N to 7d for more pack headroom. If S1 and S3 hardcode N separately, they can disagree, so a clone that S3 considers fresh may lose history that S1 already reclaimed.
findings.suggested_fix: Define one config key (e.g. `sync.reclaim_horizon_days`, default 30) consumed by both S1 and S3. Add an invariant check that the stale-clone threshold is ≤ the reclamation horizon in effect at the last swap.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a git-remote-s3 version pin and a preflight/contract test that asserts the bundle layout and push-lock semantics before the S3 adapter performs any delete.
evidence: "enumerate bundles (`get_bundles_for_ref`) ... write ONE rewritten bundle and delete the originals — deliberately BYPASSING the auto-doctor"
The core-git primitive has a preflight (`git fast-import --version`); no equivalent preflight exists for git-remote-s3
findings.finding: The S3-backend reclaim couples rebar to git-remote-s3 internals: bundle enumeration via `get_bundles_for_ref`, its push-lock implementation, the bundle-per-push storage layout, and bypassing its auto-doctor. The plan acknowledges this dependency but does not mitigate it with a version pin, a contract test, or a preflight that verifies the expected layout and lock semantics.
scenarios: A git-remote-s3 upgrade changes the bundle naming or lock semantics. The reclaim then misreads the head set, so the T0 precondition passes falsely, and the delete removes live bundles.
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the fast-import preflight: assert the git-remote-s3 version is in a tested range, and abort if the bundle listing or lock acquisition does not match the expected contract.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define rollback for the post-swap-write case (replay events added since the swap onto the restored backup), rehearse it on the shadow/canary remote, and enumerate the staged-rollout stages.
evidence: "the swap is one revertible step"
"never mutates origin/tickets or the Gerrit box until the approved staged rollout"
No post-swap-write rollback procedure or rollback rehearsal is listed
findings.finding: Rollback is described as 'one revertible step' restoring a backup ref or bundle prefix. The plan does not specify how to undo the swap after clients have reconciled onto the rewritten baseline and pushed new events, which would be lost or diverge on revert. It also does not state that the rollback is rehearsed. 'Approved staged rollout' is referenced but its stages (canary remote, then Gerrit box, then origin) are undefined.
scenarios: Hours after the swap, verify-authorship fails in CI. Reverting to `refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date>` discards every event pushed on the new baseline in the meantime, unless those events are replayed onto the restored history.
findings.suggested_fix: Rollback = restore the backup ref via the same CAS, then replay event files committed after the swap (identified by `position` > swap T0) using the same event-file replay path. Rehearse this in the S2/S2b prototype and list the rollout stages explicitly.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the client disposition: a <N-day non-FF reject is transient (replay reconcile, then retry the push); a >N-day override is a surfaced, non-silent outcome (explicit warning/exit code plus a local quarantine of the discarded events).
evidence: "S3 stale-clone detection + forced remote-override on reconnect"
"residual loss of a >N-day-drifted clone's divergent work is ACCEPTED"
No surfaced disposition for the override or for non-FF rejection is stated
findings.finding: Client-side post-swap failure arms have no stated disposition. These are: the auto-push rejected as non-FF after a rewrite, and the S3 stale-clone forced override discarding >N-day divergent work. The plan accepts the loss but never states what the user or agent sees: a silent reset, a warning, or an error/exit code, and whether the discarded events are preserved locally anywhere.
findings.location: Mechanism S3 — 'stale-clone detection + forced remote-override on reconnect'
scenarios: An agent's write is silently discarded by the override and the agent believes its ticket transition succeeded.
A <N-day clone's non-FF rejection is misclassified as fatal, which halts the write lane instead of triggering a replay reconcile.
findings.suggested_fix: Failure-disposition contract (client): non-FF after a reclaim epoch → transient, reconcile via event-file replay and re-push. A stale (>N-day) clone → forced override, surfaced as an explicit warning with a distinct exit code; divergent event files are copied to a local quarantine ref/dir before the reset.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify a rewrite-epoch signal that every clone checks before merge/push, on both git and S3 backends, so a <N-day clone always takes the event-file-replay path and never merges or pushes the old lineage.
evidence: "its non-interactive auto-doctor (`s3_doctor.py`) folds divergent heads by lossless merge and NEVER discards a head, so a normally-pushed rewrite would be MERGED BACK (resurrected)"
"Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline (append-only files, not history merge)"
"A rewrite changes every commit SHA ⇒ every clone/worktree diverges (non-FF update of a shared auto-pushed branch)"
S3 is scoped to 'stale clones (>N days)'; no rewrite-detection signal is specified for <N-day clones.
findings.finding: The plan never says how an in-horizon (<N-day) clone detects that published history was rewritten. Without that, the client's normal sync can re-attach the old lineage and resurrect the entire reclaimed history. On git remotes, a rejected non-FF auto-push followed by rebar's usual fetch+merge yields a merge commit whose parent is the old lineage. On the S3 backend, git-remote-s3 accepts the divergent bundle, and the auto-doctor 'NEVER discards a head', so it merges it back. The plan bypasses the doctor only for the swap itself, not for the subsequent client pushes. The stated client path 'reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY' has no trigger that forces replay instead of history merge.
findings.location: Feasibility — 'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline'; S3 stale-clone override (covers only >N-day clones)
scenarios: S3 backend: a 2-day-old clone auto-pushes its pre-swap head after the swap. The doctor merges it, and all reclaimed commits/trees are reachable again, so the pack returns to ~481 MiB.
Git/Gerrit remote: a clone's auto-push is rejected non-FF. Sync fetches and merges, and the merge commit reintroduces the full old history on `tickets`.
findings.suggested_fix: Publish a monotonically increasing reclaim epoch (e.g., baseline commit SHA recorded in a well-known ref or file on `tickets`). Clients compare it to their last-synced epoch before any merge or auto-push. On mismatch they switch to replay-onto-baseline and refuse to push old-lineage commits, on both git and S3 backends.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define the replay set as only event files absent from the clone's last-synced remote tree (unpushed local writes), and add a test that a <N-day clone's replay re-adds zero reclaimed files.
evidence: "Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline (append-only files, not history merge)"
"C1–C5 proven to prevent resurrection across all clone states, incl. a <N-day clone with unpushed writes."
findings.finding: The 'event-file replay' set is undefined. A <N-day clone's working tree still contains the reclaimed `.retired` and pre-fold event files. Replaying all of its event files onto the baseline would re-add exactly the files the GC deleted, which is resurrection. To be safe, the replay must be restricted to events the clone authored and never got onto the remote, e.g. local files absent from the last-synced remote-tracking tree. The plan does not state this restriction, yet the resurrection AC claims coverage for 'a <N-day clone with unpushed writes'.
findings.location: Feasibility — 'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline'; AC 'prevent resurrection across all clone states, incl. a <N-day clone with unpushed writes'
scenarios: A clone synced 3 days ago with one unpushed event replays its whole event dir onto the baseline. Hundreds of GC'd `.retired` files reappear and are pushed back.
findings.suggested_fix: Replay set = files in the local `tickets` tree that are not in the tree of the last-fetched remote-tracking ref at T0 (i.e., unpushed local writes only). Never replay files that existed at or before the clone's last sync.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile the deferred S0–S3 checkboxes with the HARD STOP. Point each item to the child ticket that completed it, and add an AC recording the human approval (who/when) that preceded the destructive rollout.
evidence: "## Deferred child-slice work (S0–S3 — NOT implemented here; only after approval)" with every item [x]
"DESIGN + PROOF only: ... none of the deferred S0–S3 items done here."
"Escalated to the orchestrator for human approval before any destructive action."
findings.finding: The ticket's checkbox state contradicts its own HARD STOP. All 'Deferred child-slice work (S0–S3 — NOT implemented here; only after approval)' items are marked [x], while the HARD STOP says none of them are done in this slice. No item records the actual human approval that gated the destructive child work. 'Escalated to a human' is not 'approved', and the operator decision selects an option, not the rollout. Nothing in the end state shows that approval preceded the history rewrite.
findings.location: Deferred child-slice work (S0–S3) checklist vs HARD STOP; AC 'Escalated to a human for approval'
scenarios: A reviewer cannot tell whether S0–S3 were executed in this slice, in violation of the HARD STOP, or in children, nor whether approval preceded the rewrite of origin/tickets.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Retitle to reflect remote-anchored history reclamation (commit/tree collapse to SNAPSHOT baseline) plus stale-clone override, with `.retired` GC as a sub-part.
evidence: "`.retired` files are blobs; the guarded pack is blobless ⇒ `.retired` GC shrinks it ~0."
"Broadened from `.retired`-only to commit/tree reclamation."
findings.finding: The title promises 'retired-event GC', but the plan's own quantification says `.retired` GC shrinks the guarded blobless pack by ~0. The actual deliverable is below-horizon commit/tree history collapse. This minor headline/body mismatch will mislead anyone scanning for the history-rewrite epic.
findings.location: Title vs 'Quantified win — insufficient alone' and S2 'Broadened from `.retired`-only to commit/tree reclamation'
scenarios: An operator searching for the ticket that rewrites `tickets` history finds only a '.retired GC' title and misjudges its blast radius.
findings.suggested_fix: Retitle: 'Remote-anchored history reclamation (below-horizon commit/tree collapse + .retired GC) + stale-clone override (N-day horizon)'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the reclaim-detection signal: an epoch record in the baseline tree whose lineage names the epoch it replaces, proven by verifiable provenance. Clones override only when the remote epoch provably supersedes the local one, and staleness is classified from the local unpushed events' age, not from merge-base.
evidence: "A rewrite changes every commit SHA ⇒ every clone/worktree diverges"
"S3 stale-clone detection + forced remote-override on reconnect" — no detection signal is named
src/rebar/_store/sync.py:113-123 refuses to merge an unrelated history when the local store carries ticket events
findings.finding: The plan does not say how a clone recognises that a reclaim happened, or how it tells a <N-day clone from a >N-day one. A rewrite changes every commit SHA, so no existing clone shares any ancestor with the new graph. Merge-base or ancestry checks would therefore class every clone as stale and force-reset it, losing in-horizon unpushed work that the plan says is preserved. Without a marker, today's sync.py refuses unrelated histories that already carry ticket events and logs DIVERGED, so every clone gets stuck. If clones instead auto-reset onto any unrelated remote history, anyone with push access could force-push an arbitrary history and every clone would adopt it with reset --hard.
findings.location: Feasibility — 'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY'; Mechanism S3; Boundary C3
scenarios: A clone that synced 2 days ago with unpushed writes reconnects. The plan gives no way to tell it apart from a 40-day-stale clone.
A compromised or mistaken force-push to sync.remote is adopted by every clone if the reset is triggered just by 'no common ancestor'.
findings.suggested_fix: Have S2 write a store-epoch record into the checkpoint tree with a new epoch id and an epoch_lineage naming the replaced epoch, signed or otherwise verifiable. In S3, the reconnect path runs the override only when the remote epoch supersedes the local one; any other unrelated history keeps the DIVERGED refusal. Define stale as: the oldest unpushed local event is older than the horizon.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define 'unpushed' as an event whose uuid is unknown to the remote tip: absent under its ticket dir with any suffix AND absent from every remote SNAPSHOT's source_event_uuids. Never replay local SNAPSHOTs, and replay the original blobs byte-identically.
evidence: "Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline" — the unpushed predicate is unspecified
Boundary C1 relies on SNAPSHOT folding plus `.retired` renames, so the same event uuid can exist under different filenames or only inside a SNAPSHOT
findings.finding: Event-file replay does not define which local files count as 'unpushed'. Replaying files that exist locally but not at the remote tip (set difference) brings back folded events. A <N-day clone may hold a live event file X.json that the remote has since compacted, either retired to X.json.retired or dropped from the baseline and folded into a SNAPSHOT. Set-difference replay re-adds X.json next to the SNAPSHOT that already folds it, so the event is applied twice. Replaying the clone's local SNAPSHOT files would also overwrite the rewritten ledger annotations.
findings.location: Feasibility — 'EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline (append-only files, not history merge)'
scenarios: Compaction retires X on the remote 1 day before the swap. A clone that last fetched 3 days ago replays X.json and the event is resurrected.
A clone replays its local SNAPSHOT, which carries pre-rewrite commit_sha annotations.
findings.suggested_fix: In the replay step, compute the known-uuid set per ticket from remote tip filenames (.json and .json.retired) plus each remote SNAPSHOT's data.source_event_uuids. Replay only non-SNAPSHOT local events outside that set, staging the original blob ids at their live paths in one commit. Back up the old local tip to a local-only ref first.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Consider resolving ledger position→commit on the current graph at verify time instead of rewriting SNAPSHOT bytes. If annotations must still be rewritten, name the signer/key, the keyring era that must contain it, and how clones holding the old SNAPSHOT bytes reconcile.
evidence: "The same S2 pass re-resolves position→commit_sha in the NEW graph, rewrites the SNAPSHOT ledger annotations"
"S2 coalesce to a re-signed baseline checkpoint" — no signer or key era is specified
src/rebar/_commands/verify_authorship.py:366-367 reads the ledger's stored position.commit_sha into the scoped event used for the era check
"the authorship_ledger keys on the stable `position` ({ts}-{uuid}), invariant across the rewrite"
findings.finding: Reconciling the ledger by rewriting SNAPSHOT `authorship_ledger` commit_sha annotations means rewriting event blobs in place, at the same filename with different bytes, including above-horizon SNAPSHOTs that clones already hold. This conflicts with the I1/I2 append-only, globally-unique-filename doctrine the proof relies on. It gives every <N-day clone a same-path, different-content file that any union merge or replay will conflict on. It also forces a 're-signed baseline' without naming the signer, the key, or which keyring era must hold that key. A simpler alternative exists: treat the stored commit_sha as a cache, and have the verifier resolve position→commit on the current graph (falling back to the stored value only if unresolved). Positions are already invariant and globally unique, as the plan notes. With that, no event blob changes, no re-signing is needed, and verification is the same on both graphs.
findings.location: Feasibility — Ledger reconciliation (G6); Mechanism S2 ('re-signed baseline checkpoint')
scenarios: A clone that has the old SNAPSHOT bytes unions or replays against the rewritten SNAPSHOT and gets a conflict or an overwrite.
The re-signing key is not valid at the checkpoint era, so verify-identity fails on the rewritten graph.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile the quantification: give the commit-rate window behind ~14K/day, label each figure as either saving or remaining size, and state the positive rationale for running the reclaim before or after W1/W2.
evidence: "235,482 commits ... ~14K commits/day"
"Max safe win N=30d ≈ 365–380 MiB; N=7d ≈ 200–215 MiB; ≤100 MiB needs an unsafe <4-day horizon"
docs/adr/0106-remote-anchored-history-reclamation.md:195 "At the default N=30d horizon the retained graph is still ~365–380 MiB"
findings.finding: The measured figures that justify fitness and sequencing contradict each other. 235,482 total commits at ~14K commits/day means about 17 days of history at that rate, so a 30-day horizon would reclaim almost nothing unless the rate is recent. 'Max safe win N=30d ≈ 365–380 MiB' reads as a saving (481 → ~100–115 MiB). That conflicts with '≤100 MiB needs an unsafe <4-day horizon' and with the ADR, which gives 365–380 MiB as what remains after the reclaim. Because the reclaim at N=30d only cuts about 100 MiB, and W1/W2 are named as the durable fix, the plan should state why it pays for a high-blast-radius shared-branch rewrite now, before W1/W2. Running the reclaim after W1/W2 would collapse the whole pre-shard, pre-batching heavy history in one rewrite and could leave a much smaller remainder.
scenarios: An approver reads 'win ≈ 365–380 MiB' as nearly reaching the budget and approves a destructive rewrite whose real saving is about 100 MiB.
The rewrite runs before W1/W2 and has to be repeated after them to get a meaningful reduction.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Cite the established grace-horizon prior art (Cassandra gc_grace_seconds plus wipe-and-rebootstrap of stale replicas; CRDT causal-stability GC) in the DESIGN + PROOF, and derive N from its 'max offline + reconcile interval' sizing rule.
evidence: Plan: "(C2) that fold reachable on the sync remote's `tickets` ref ≥ N days, (C3) stale clones (>N days) forced to reset to remote"
DataStax docs (retrieved): if a node is down past the grace period, "you must remove all Cassandra data from it and perform a node replacement"
AxonOps docs (retrieved): "gc_grace_seconds must exceed maximum expected node downtime plus repair interval."
The plan text has no prior-art reference for the horizon/override design; the citations it mentions point to in-repo invariants only.
findings.finding: The remote-anchored N-day horizon with forced reset of stale clones (C2/C3) is an established pattern: Cassandra's gc_grace_seconds tombstone purge with mandatory wipe-and-rebootstrap of replicas down longer than the grace period, and causal-stability GC in CRDTs. The plan presents it without citing that prior art or adopting its known operating rules, for example that the horizon must exceed maximum expected offline time plus the reconcile interval.
scenarios: N=30d is picked without the 'max offline time + reconcile interval' sizing rule, and a clone that was offline just under N but behind on reconcile still resurrects data.
Known failure modes of the pattern (clock skew, a replica that misses the purge window) are rediscovered in S3 rather than designed for.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how a client detects the rewrite (for example, a published baseline marker or rewrite-epoch ref that the client checks on fetch) and how it reconciles by replaying event files for clones fewer than N days behind. Require this client version to be deployed everywhere and confirmed before the swap, with a gate that refuses old clients.
evidence: 'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline (append-only files, not history merge)'
'S3 stale-clone detection + forced remote-override on reconnect' (covers only >N-day clones)
'every clone/worktree diverges (non-FF update of a shared auto-pushed branch)'
No deploy-ordering or version-gate step between the client-side reconcile code and the swap
findings.finding: The plan does not specify how clones and worktrees that are fewer than N days behind detect the rewrite and switch to event-file replay. It also does not require that this client behavior ship and be deployed before the swap, which is the expand-contract order. Clones today auto-push and sync with normal git. A clone that has not been upgraded will see a non-fast-forward, fetch, and merge, which makes the entire pre-rewrite history an ancestor again. That undoes the reclaim (and the pack shrink) and pushes the reclaimed commits back to `tickets`. S3 covers only clones more than N days stale.
findings.location: Feasibility — 'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline'; S3 stale-clone override
scenarios: A developer laptop or worktree running an older rebar holds unpushed writes from yesterday. After the swap its sync merges the old history back in and auto-pushes, so the old commits and trees come back on `tickets`.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'reclaim epoch' marker ref or file that the swap advances. Make sync compare its local epoch with the remote's. On a mismatch, sync hard-resets to the remote and replays local event files that are not on the remote, and never runs a git merge. Ship and deploy this (expand) before any swap (contract), and record a minimum client version that the remote/CI gate enforces.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define rollback as compensating-forward. Restore the backup ref plus `enforce_since`, replay every event file committed since the swap onto the restored history, and assert the post-rollback state: the set of event files is a superset of the pre-rollback tip's, `rebar fsck` and verify-authorship are clean, and clones reconcile back by replay. Mark the plan DATA LOSS RISK until this is done.
evidence: 'Rollback: immutable backup ref refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date> (or the S3 rollback bundle prefix) before the swap'
'the swap is one revertible step'
No post-rollback assertion (event-set equality, verify-authorship green, clone reconcile direction) and no handling of post-swap writes
findings.finding: The rollback steps say only that the swap is 'one revertible step' back to the backup ref. The plan never states what persisted state must hold after a rollback. Once the swap is published, clones reconcile onto the new baseline and auto-push new events as commits on the rewritten history. Resetting `tickets` to `refs/tickets-backup/...` throws away those commits. Clones that already reconciled would diverge again and could run the replay or override path in the opposite direction. The re-signed SNAPSHOT ledger annotations and `enforce_since` would also need to be restored together. DATA LOSS RISK: writes acknowledged after the swap and before a rollback are lost unless they are replayed forward onto the restored history.
scenarios: The swap succeeds. Over the next six hours, 3,500 events are pushed on top of the new history. Verify Authorship then fails and operators roll back to the backup ref, losing those 3,500 events.
findings.suggested_fix: Rollback procedure: (1) take a snapshot of the current rewritten tip; (2) diff its event files against the backup tip; (3) create a commit on top of the backup ref carrying the post-swap event files; (4) publish it with a CAS against the current rewritten tip; (5) revert the enforce_since anchor and bump the reclaim epoch so clones replay again; (6) assert fsck, verify-authorship, and event-set coverage.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Remove the §I1-promotion AC from 866f, or mark it superseded by 596a, so exactly one child owns the 'I1 moved to implemented' outcome.
evidence: 866f AC: '[x] `docs/concurrency.md` §I1 is promoted from 'follow-up' to implemented and cross-references ADR 0106.'
866f Verification: '`grep -n 'ADR 0106\|implemented' docs/concurrency.md` confirms the §I1 promotion' (a loose grep that any occurrence of 'implemented' satisfies)
596a Why: 'On origin/main 9d10232dd89 ... docs/concurrency.md §I1 (lines 61-75) still says the reclamation "is specified by **ADR 0106**"' and ADR Follow-up 'still says "*specified, in-progress*"'
596a step 2 rewrites ADR 0106's Follow-up to say I1 'is promoted from a *follow-up* to an *implemented* model'
findings.finding: 866f (closed, all ACs checked) and 596a both own the same parent outcome: 'docs/concurrency.md §I1 promoted from follow-up to implemented and cross-references ADR 0106'. 596a's evidence shows that 866f's checked AC was not true when checked: on origin/main §I1 still said the reclamation 'is specified by ADR 0106'. Two siblings claim the same deliverable, and one claims it falsely.
scenarios: A completion verifier counts 866f as covering the parent's 'docs/concurrency.md §I1 moved to implemented' box, even though the text was not changed until 596a.
Future readers trust 866f's checked AC and weak grep as proof of promotion.
findings.suggested_fix: Strike or annotate 866f's last AC as 'superseded by 596a-8b1b-299e-49e1 (the ADR only cross-references; promotion landed in 596a)', and add a comment on 866f recording this.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile f04e with the parent C1–C5 proof: amend ADR 0106 for re-signing (attribution change, author_id injection), and make sure the human go/no-go covered the re-signed rewrite.
evidence: Parent: 'Under C1–C5: no still-observable state changes, no signature verification breaks, no resurrection.' C4 = signature 'carried in the SNAPSHOT authorship_ledger OR enforce_since re-anchored'

f04e: 're-sign every failing event during the rewrite with the bot key ... and give the 253 events `author_id` 594c'; '1,435 raw and 6,070 SNAPSHOT-ledger events signed by keys not on identity 594c's keyring'
f04e AC: 'reduced state of the rewritten history equals the original apart from `authorship` counts and the added `author_id`s'
f04e: '`reclaim_dry_run.py` is unchanged (its equality checks assume a verdict-preserving collapse); the real-data proof uses an out-of-repo driver'
8dc4: 'The reclaim must not change any event's verdict'; bdf3 AC: 'all still-observable ticket state are bit-identical in reduced form'
findings.finding: f04e re-signs failing events during the collapse. It sets missing author_id, rewrites raw event bytes and replaces ledger signatures with a bot key. This contradicts the parent's proven C1–C5 guarantees ('no still-observable state changes, no signature verification breaks'). It also contradicts siblings that assume a verdict- and state-preserving rewrite: bdf3 (reduced state bit-identical), 8dc4 (same per-verdict counts before and after) and 866f (ADR proof of I1–I9 under carriage + re-anchor only). f04e's real-data proof deliberately bypasses the 8dc4 harness by using an out-of-repo driver, and it has no AC that escalates the re-signed variant to a human before the swap.
scenarios: The production reclaim recorded in 596a used the re-signed collapse, but the human go/no-go evidence (8dc4's evidence.json) described a verdict-preserving collapse.
Events originally signed by keys outside the keyring now carry a bot signature, which changes attribution. No ADR amendment proves this keeps I1–I9 or the authorship model sound.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an f04e AC (or a follow-up child) that amends ADR 0106 §4 to document re-signing as a sanctioned C4 path with its attribution consequences, and that posts the re-signed run's evidence for explicit human approval before any publish.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a child (or ACs on an existing one) for the production swap: recorded human approval, pre-swap shadow fsck/replay/verify-authorship, post-swap green Verify Authorship Identity run plus full reconcile, and a backup-ref retention rule.
evidence: Parent Risk/rollback: 'never prune the backup until a green Verify Authorship Identity run + full reconcile'
Parent HARD STOP: 'never mutates origin/tickets or the Gerrit box until the approved staged rollout'
8dc4 AC: 'escalated to a human for the pre-swap go/no-go. No production swap is executed.'
